chapter: Postwar years, accident and lean times
title: The 'Jealous Woman Blues' date with no drums for Frankie's label
summary: At a Sansom Street Philadelphia club a young Italian fan arranged a recording for the Mammoth label, but the new drummer lacked drums, and Autrey considers it the worst date of his career.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: -- I think it would be kind of nice, because I met a nice little guy, little Italian fellow, Frankie -- what was Frankie's last name? Anyways, he was
very nice.
This was in Philadelphia, now?
Philadelphia, uh-huh. And he came by the club, the Trouville Club?
Not in Philadelphia.

No, not in Philadelphia, Trouville, this is a -- the -- uh, uh, on Sansom Street, in Philadelphia, yeah, between 15th and 16th on Sansom Street. Uh, Uh, I'll think of the name of it in a minute. Stayed there long enough.
(Laughter.)

And this guy liked our -- liked our group, and he wrote a couple of things, and had a few tunes he wanted me to do, and we recorded them. In fact, he and somebody at one of the stations there got together and brought the group over, and I had -- oh, did I have my troubles! I had just hired a drummer to come in with us to play, and he had been working with Lionel Hampton, he told me, and I didn't know but what he -- what a drummer! Oh, he was terrific.

And he said well what made him -- he kept telling me a story, well, I left my drums over here. I'll pick them up tomorrow, and so forth, and so I said well okay, you know. Time -- I figured the drummer man's been working night, with somebody like Hamp, I mean you don't question those people. Do you read? Do you play? Or what happened? I mean it's
just one of those things a man is caught up, and he'll be all right tomorrow, the next day.

So I -- I got a date to record, and he didn't have any drums. He couldn't get his drums because he'd left them here, left them there, so I went out to try to borry him some drums. I tried to rent him some drums. Nothing I did would work, for some reason or other they had no more drums to rent. I said well look, here's -- I'll give you whatever money you want. Here's a hundred dollars. Let me rent the drums so we can record. A couple of hours went on, no, we can't do that, or we don't do that, or we don't have -- I -- for some reason it didn't work.

So I went on the date. Didn't have any drums. And we had to run from -- after we got in there we had to go into a darkened room, a room with no mikes, and no windows. Nobody could see what you're doing. Had to run down steps, around this wing, and come into there, and run back, and we -- and that's the way the thing went down there, it was awful. It was the worst I've ever done, and I've been recording -- had been recording for years.

So we did a blues, and what else? We did a couple of things. Eeh, 'Jealous Woman Blues.' That's one -- that's the title of the date, I think, one tune, anyway. Bah, bah-de-bahma, bah, bah bah, it was awful. And it only was -- always -- it was printed, and I'm very sorry, more, not for
my sake, for Frankie, because this was a man, he was such a nice little guy, and he wanted everything to go right, and go wrong -- it went wrong, and I haven't seen him since.
(Laughs.) Were the records released?
Uhm uh-huh, yes. I got to -- I think have the record, or one of them, around here somewhere. Or I had one, anyway.
What's the label? Do you remember?
Yeah, 'Jealous Woman Blues.'
No, I mean what's the company (inaudible).
Uh, Mammoth --
Mammoth? Monmouth? Mammoth?
Something like that, yeah. Yeah, Mammoth. Yeah, Mammoth.
Was this the first recording you'd done with your own group, with you as leader?
I think so, by golly! I really do.
When would this be? In the middle forties?
Well, yeah.

Yeah, yeah, yes. This is after Pats passed, or before? After, I think it was after. I think, you know. And -- well, and nothing happened, with the recording. I -- this (unintelligible) but I thought I'd mention it,
